query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment that promotes the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent CrTaO4-based oxide scale on the surface of a refractory high‐entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., a Ti–V–Nb–Ta alloy) in its as‐cast or synthesized state without a preformed protective oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Apply a pre-oxidation heat treatment at around 1100°C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere to induce rapid formation of a dense CrTaO4-based surface oxide.
generation.conditions: The treatment is intended for environments at or above 1100°C with an oxygen-containing atmosphere, and its benefits should manifest under prolonged exposure (e.g., up to 200 hours of isothermal oxidation).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense, continuous CrTaO4-based oxide scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed CrTaO4 scale acts as an effective diffusion barrier that minimizes oxygen ingress and subsequent oxidation of the underlying alloy, preserving its structural integrity under extreme temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an untreated alloy, the pre-oxidized sample should show a significantly reduced oxygen uptake (lower weight gain) and a more uniform, protective oxide scale, thereby enhancing high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: An untreated refractory high-entropy alloy exposed directly to high-temperature oxygen results in less protective or discontinuous oxide layers, leading to higher oxidation rates and material degradation.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected to be significant only in regimes where the CrTaO4 phase is thermodynamically favored (around 1100°C and in oxygen-rich conditions) and may not apply at considerably lower temperatures or different atmospheric conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in oxygen resistance is not yet determined and may depend on the specific alloy composition and exact pre-oxidation parameters. Optimization and reproducibility of the dense CrTaO4 scale formation remain to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same refractory high-entropy alloy. Subject one set to a pre-oxidation heat treatment at 1100°C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere for a duration sufficient to form the protective CrTaO4-based scale, and leave the other set untreated. Then expose both sets to continuous oxidation at 1100°C in air for 200 hours.
measurements: Thermogravimetric analysis to track weight gain during oxidation
Microscopic and spectroscopic analysis (e.g., SEM/EDS, XRD) to assess the morphology and composition of the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in weight gain and do not show the formation of a dense, adherent CrTaO4-based oxide scale relative to untreated samples—i.e., if their oxidation behavior is comparable or worse—the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide

Abstract: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours.
